lessons.title: Getting Exposure Through Mutual Funds and ETFs: Sector Funds, Consumption, and Low Volatility Indices

body.text: A fund's name tells you its theme, not its cyclicality. India's best-known consumption index has almost as much in autos and consumer durables as in FMCG, and the low volatility index picks stocks by how calmly their prices move, not by how stable their earnings are. Read the holdings, not the label.

children.text: Most Indian investors get their cyclical and defensive exposure through funds rather than direct stocks. That is usually sensible, but it introduces a new problem: you are now trusting somebody else's definition of a theme. This lesson goes through the main routes, opens up two popular index products to show what is really inside them, and covers the costs and mechanics that decide how much of the return reaches you.

children.text: Sectoral and Thematic Funds: The Rules That Bind Them

Under SEBI's categorisation rules, a sectoral or thematic fund must keep at least 80% of its assets in that sector or theme. This matters more than it sounds. If you buy a pharma fund and pharma has a bad three years, the manager cannot rescue you by moving into banks. The sector call is yours, and so is the responsibility for timing it. SEBI has also been tightening this space: its updated classification rules separate sectoral funds from thematic funds and limit how much a sectoral or thematic scheme's portfolio can overlap with other equity schemes from the same fund house, which is meant to stop near-identical funds being sold as different products.

body.text: Chapter 5 showed leadership reversing violently: Nifty IT returned 59.6% in 2021 and then fell 26.0% in 2022, and Nifty Pharma lost money four years running before returning 60.6% in 2020. Sectoral funds are usually marketed hardest after the good years. The 80% rule means the fund cannot step aside when the cycle turns, so your entry point does most of the work.

children.text: Consumption funds are often pitched as a way to own India's growing middle class, and many investors assume that means staples. The Nifty India Consumption index holds 30 companies that earn more than half their revenue domestically, spread across nine sectors, with a 10% cap on any single stock at rebalancing. Here is roughly how those weights have been distributed.

body.title: How Cyclical Is Consumption?
body.prompt: Using the weights above, add the automobile and auto components weight to the consumer durables weight. What percentage of the index sits in these two early cyclical groups? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 20.06 + 16.1 = 36.2%. That is essentially the same weight as FMCG at 35.9%. Cars and washing machines are postponable purchases that respond to EMIs, so a consumption fund is a blend of defensive staples and early cyclicals, not a defensive holding.

children.text: Add consumer services, media, and textiles, all discretionary, and close to 46% of the index responds to how confident households feel. That is not a flaw in the index. It is an accurate picture of Indian consumption. But an investor who bought it expecting soap-and-toothpaste stability would be surprised in a slowdown.
The Low Volatility Factor: Price Calm, Not Earnings Calm

markDefs.definition: An index that selects and weights stocks using a rule based on a measurable characteristic, such as low volatility, quality, value, or momentum, instead of market capitalisation alone.

children.text: The Nifty 100 Low Volatility 30 is a

. It starts with the Nifty 100, measures each stock's volatility as the standard deviation of its daily returns over the past year, ranks them, and holds the 30 least volatile. Weights are set in inverse proportion to volatility, so the calmest stocks get the most weight, with a cap for less liquid names. It is rebalanced periodically, so the holdings change as market behaviour changes.

In practice this often lands on staples, pharma, and utilities, which is why it feels defensive. But notice what the rule actually measures: price movement, the exact thing Chapter 1 warned was the wrong test. A stock can have calm prices and cyclical earnings, or volatile prices and rock-solid earnings. The index also reselects after the fact, so a sector whose prices have been calm recently gets in, even if its earnings risk is rising.

body.title: Which Gives Earnings Defensiveness?
body.question: You want exposure to businesses whose profits hold up in a slowdown. Which choice most directly targets that?
options: A low volatility index fund, because it selects the least volatile stocks
A consumption thematic fund, because consumption is non-discretionary
A staples-focused fund or a set of companies with stable earnings through past slowdowns
A broad Nifty 50 index fund, because it is diversified
body.explanation: Low volatility selects on price movement, and a consumption index holds about 36% in autos and consumer durables. Only choosing businesses with proven earnings stability targets earnings defensiveness directly. The Nifty 50 gives you the market's own mix, which includes plenty of cyclicals.

stats.label: Cost of 1 percentage point a year
stats.context: On a ₹10,000 monthly SIP over 20 years, comparing 12% with 11% returns

children.text: Invest ₹10,000 a month for 20 years, a total of ₹24 lakh. Compounding at 12% a year, the corpus reaches about ₹99.9 lakh. At 11%, it reaches about ₹87.4 lakh. The single percentage point difference costs about ₹12.6 lakh, more than half of everything you contributed.

This is why cost deserves the same attention as sector selection. It is also why a high-fee sectoral fund needs to be right about the cycle by a meaningful margin just to match a cheap diversified fund. SEBI caps expense ratios on a sliding scale that falls as a scheme grows, and from April 2026 fund houses disclose the management fee separately from brokerage and statutory charges, which makes comparison easier.

Two mechanical points matter for ETFs specifically. First, you buy them on the exchange, so you pay the spread between bid and ask prices, which can be wide on thinly traded sectoral or international ETFs and can quietly cost more than a year of expense ratio. Second, an ETF's market price can drift from its underlying value when trading is thin, so check volumes before choosing an ETF over an index fund.

body.title: The Rule That Binds
body.textWithBlank: SEBI requires a sectoral or thematic fund to hold at least ___ percent of its assets in that sector or theme, which is why the manager cannot move to safety when the cycle turns.
body.explanation: The 80% floor is what makes these funds a direct bet on your own sector view and timing, rather than on the manager's flexibility.

body.title: The Defensive Fund That Isn't
body.scenario: Shalini expects a consumer slowdown and wants to make her equity portfolio more defensive. She already holds a flexi-cap fund and a Nifty 50 index fund. Her plan is to move 30% of her equity into a consumption fund, because 'people always need to consume', and another 10% into a low volatility index fund, because 'low volatility means safe'. She has not looked at either portfolio.
body.prompt: What would you point out before she invests?
body.modelAnswer: Both labels are doing more work than the products. The consumption index carries about 36% in autos and consumer durables and close to 46% in discretionary categories overall, so in a consumer slowdown a large part of it is exposed to exactly the demand she is worried about; it is a blend, not a defensive. The low volatility index does often hold defensive-looking names, but it selects on past price volatility rather than earnings stability, so it is a backward-looking rule, and calm prices do not guarantee calm profits. She should also check overlap: her flexi-cap and Nifty 50 funds already hold many of the same large caps, so adding 40% across two more products may concentrate her in a handful of names rather than diversifying. Practical steps: read both index methodology documents and the fund factsheets, list the top holdings and sector weights, and compare them with what she already owns. If she genuinely wants earnings defensiveness, a staples-heavy fund or a set of companies with stable profits through past slowdowns targets it more directly, and she should size it against the mix she set in the previous lesson.

body.title: Check What a Fund Actually Holds
steps: Open the latest factsheet and note the sector allocation, not just the fund name
List the top 10 holdings and classify each using the Chapter 1 scorecard
For an index product, read the index methodology document: what rule selects the stocks, and how often it rebalances
Compare the holdings with the funds you already own to find overlap
Check the expense ratio of the direct plan, and for ETFs check traded volumes and spreads
For a sectoral fund, check where that sector sits in its own return cycle before investing
Decide how the holding fits your target cyclical and defensive mix, and size it accordingly

points: Fund labels describe themes, not cyclicality; the holdings decide how a fund behaves in a downturn
SEBI requires sectoral and thematic funds to keep at least 80% in their sector or theme, so the manager cannot step aside when the cycle turns
The Nifty India Consumption index holds about 36% in autos and consumer durables against about 36% in FMCG, making it a blend rather than a defensive
The low volatility factor selects on past price movement, not earnings stability, which is the distinction this course started with
Costs compound: one percentage point a year on a ₹10,000 monthly SIP over 20 years is worth about ₹12.6 lakh
For ETFs, check traded volumes and bid-ask spreads, which can cost more than the expense ratio on thin sectoral products

body.text: Index sector weights are as published in the index provider's material consulted at the time of writing and change at every rebalancing, so check the current factsheet before relying on them. Regulatory details, expense ratio norms, and disclosure rules can change. The SIP cost illustration assumes constant annual returns of 12% and 11%, which real funds do not deliver. Shalini's scenario is illustrative. This lesson is educational and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security, fund, or index product.
